claims.text: Why cranial nerve signs localize: one-sided leg weakness with upper motor neuron signs can come from anywhere between the cortex and the lumbar spine, but an abnormal cranial nerve sign alongside it strongly suggests a brain stem cause.
claims.quote: For example, unilateral leg weakness with upper motor signs may be due to pathology anywhere between the cerebral cortex and the lumbar spine. However, the presence of an abnormal cranial nerve sign strongly suggests that the observed weakness results from a problem in the brain stem.

claims.text: Inside or outside the brain stem: long tract signs (spasticity, sensory loss below the head and neck) point to an intra-axial lesion; isolated cranial neuropathies are more likely, but not always, extra-axial.
claims.quote: In general, the presence of long tract signs such as spasticity or sensory loss below the head and neck indicate intra-axial lesions. Isolated cranial neuropathies are more likely, but not always, extra-axial.

claims.text: Cranial nerve I: the patient identifies odors (soap, coffee, cloves) presented to each nostril with the other nostril occluded.
claims.quote: The patient is asked to identify odors (eg, soap, coffee, cloves) presented to each nostril while the other nostril is occluded.

claims.text: Cranial nerve II: visual acuity in each eye separately (Snellen chart for distance, handheld chart for near), color plates, confrontation visual fields in all 4 quadrants, direct and consensual pupillary responses, and funduscopy.
claims.quote: For the optic cranial nerve (II), visual acuity is tested using a Snellen chart for distance vision or a handheld chart for near vision; each eye is assessed individually, with the other eye covered. Color perception is tested using standard pseudoisochromatic Ishihara or Hardy-Rand-Ritter plates that have numbers or figures embedded in a field of specifically colored dots. Visual fields are tested by directed confrontation in all 4 visual quadrants. Direct and consensual pupillary responses are tested. Funduscopic examination is also done.

claims.text: Cranial nerves III, IV, VI: look for ptosis, globe position and asymmetric movement; the patient follows a target to all 4 quadrants and toward the tip of the nose; brief fine nystagmus at end-lateral gaze is normal.
claims.quote: For the oculomotor, trochlear, and abducens cranial nerves (III, IV, and VI, respectively), eyes are observed for symmetry of movement, globe position, asymmetry or droop of the eyelids (ptosis), and twitches or flutters of globes or lids. Extraocular movements controlled by these nerves are tested by asking the patient to follow a moving target (eg, examiner’s finger, penlight) to all 4 quadrants (including across the midline) and toward the tip of the nose; this test can detect nystagmus and palsies of ocular muscles. Brief fine amplitude nystagmus at end-lateral gaze is normal.

claims.text: Third nerve palsy: diplopia and ptosis; the eye sits slightly out and down, adducts slowly (may not pass midline) and cannot look up well; the pupil may be normal or dilated with a sluggish or absent light response, and mydriasis may be an early sign.
claims.quote: Diplopia and ptosis (drooping of the upper eyelid) occur. The affected eye may deviate slightly out and down in straight-ahead gaze; adduction is slow and may not proceed past the midline. Upward gaze is impaired. When downward gaze is attempted, the superior oblique muscle causes the eye to adduct slightly and rotate. The pupil may be normal or dilated; its response to direct and to consensual light may be sluggish or absent (efferent defect). Mydriasis (pupil dilation) may be an early sign.
claims.locator: Symptoms and Signs of Third Cranial Nerve Disorders

claims.text: Pupil involved vs spared: third nerve palsies that affect the pupil commonly come from an aneurysm (especially posterior communicating artery) or transtentorial herniation; pupil-sparing palsies most often from ischemia of the nerve (usually diabetes or hypertension) or midbrain.
claims.quote: Third cranial (oculomotor) nerve disorders that cause palsies and affect the pupil commonly result from Aneurysms (especially of the posterior communicating artery) Transtentorial brain herniation Less commonly, meningitis affecting the brain stem (eg, tuberculosis meningitis) The most common cause of palsies that spare the pupil, particularly partial palsies, is Ischemia of the third cranial nerve (usually due to diabetes or hypertension) or of the midbrain
claims.locator: Etiology of Third Cranial Nerve Disorders

claims.text: Third nerve red flag: a dilated pupil with sudden severe headache (possible ruptured aneurysm) or increasing unresponsiveness (possible herniation) needs immediate CT or MRI.
claims.quote: If a patient has a dilated pupil and a sudden, severe headache (suggesting ruptured aneurysm) or is increasingly unresponsive (suggesting herniation), neuroimaging (CT or, if available, MRI) is done immediately.
claims.locator: Diagnosis of Third Cranial Nerve Disorders

claims.text: Fourth nerve palsy: superior oblique weakness gives double images one above and slightly beside the other, so going down stairs is hard; tilting the head to the side opposite the palsied muscle compensates.
claims.quote: Fourth cranial nerve palsy may affect one or both eyes. Because the superior oblique muscle is paretic, the eyes do not adduct normally. Patients see double images, one above and slightly to the side of the other; thus, going down stairs, which requires looking down and inward, is difficult. However, tilting the head to the side opposite the palsied muscle can compensate and eliminate the double images.

claims.text: Fourth nerve palsy cause: closed head injury is common and can cause a unilateral or bilateral palsy.
claims.quote: Closed head injury (common), which may cause a unilateral or bilateral palsy

claims.text: Sixth nerve palsy: horizontal diplopia when looking toward the paretic side; the eye rests slightly adducted (unopposed medial rectus) and abducts sluggishly, and with complete paralysis cannot abduct past midline.
claims.quote: Symptoms of sixth cranial nerve palsy include binocular horizontal diplopia when looking to the side of the paretic eye. Because the tonic action of the medial rectus muscle is unopposed, the eye is slightly adducted when the patient looks straight ahead. The eye abducts sluggishly, and even when abduction is maximal, the lateral sclera is exposed. With complete paralysis, the eye cannot abduct past midline.
claims.locator: Symptoms and Signs of Sixth Cranial Nerve Palsy

claims.text: Sixth nerve palsy causes: typically small-vessel or microvascular disease (diabetes, hypertension), compression in the cavernous sinus, orbit or skull base, or increased intracranial pressure.
claims.quote: Typically, small-vessel disease, particularly in patients with diabetes as part of a disorder called mononeuritis multiplex (multiple mononeuropathy) Microvascular disease secondary to diabetes or hypertension Compression of the nerve by lesions in the cavernous sinus (eg, nasopharyngeal tumors), orbit (eg, orbital cellulitis), or base of the skull Increased intracranial pressure (ICP)
claims.locator: Etiology of Sixth Cranial Nerve Palsy

claims.text: Cranial nerve V sensory: test sharp sensation in the 3 divisions (ophthalmic, maxillary, mandibular) and the corneal reflex; if facial sensation is lost, sparing of the jaw angle (spinal root C2) suggests a trigeminal deficit.
claims.quote: For the trigeminal cranial nerve (V), the 3 sensory divisions (ophthalmic, maxillary, mandibular) are evaluated by using a sharp object to test facial sensation and by brushing a wisp of cotton against the lower or lateral cornea to evaluate the corneal reflex. If facial sensation is lost, the angle of the jaw should be examined; sparing of this area (innervated by spinal root C2) suggests a trigeminal deficit.

claims.text: Cranial nerve V motor: palpate the masseters while the patient clenches and have the patient open against resistance; the jaw deviates toward a weak pterygoid.
claims.quote: Trigeminal motor function is tested by palpating the masseter muscles while the patient clenches the teeth and by asking the patient to open the mouth against resistance. If a pterygoid muscle is weak, the jaw deviates to that side when the mouth is opened.

claims.text: Central vs peripheral facial weakness: the weak side shows a flattened nasolabial fold and a wider palpebral fissure; if only the lower face is weak (forehead furrowing and eye closure preserved), the cause is central rather than peripheral.
claims.quote: The nasolabial fold is depressed and the palpebral fissure is widened on the weakened side. If the patient has only lower facial weakness (ie, furrowing of the forehead and eye closure are preserved), the etiology of the weakness in cranial nerve VII is central rather than peripheral.

claims.text: Why the forehead is spared centrally: central (cortical) input to the upper face is often bilateral, so upper-face paralysis is more likely from a peripheral facial nerve lesion than from a central lesion such as stroke.
claims.quote: The facial muscles are innervated peripherally (infranuclear innervation) by the ipsilateral seventh cranial nerve and centrally (supranuclear innervation) by the contralateral cerebral cortex. Central innervation is often bilateral for the upper face (eg, forehead muscles) and unilateral for the lower face. As a result, both central and peripheral lesions can paralyze the lower face. However, paralysis of the upper face is more likely due to peripheral lesions (facial nerve palsy) than to central lesions (eg, stroke).

claims.text: Peripheral facial palsy: the affected side is flat and expressionless, with little or no ability to wrinkle the forehead, blink or grimace; in severe cases the eye does not close.
claims.quote: The affected side becomes flat and expressionless; the ability to wrinkle the forehead, blink, and grimace is limited or absent. In severe cases, the palpebral fissure widens and the eye does not close, often irritating the conjunctiva and drying the cornea.
claims.locator: Symptoms and Signs of Facial Nerve Palsy

claims.text: Lesion above the geniculate ganglion: salivation, taste and lacrimation may also be impaired, with hyperacusis.
claims.quote: If the nerve lesion is proximal to the geniculate ganglion, salivation, taste, and lacrimation may be impaired, and hyperacusis may be present.
claims.locator: Symptoms and Signs of Facial Nerve Palsy

claims.text: Cranial nerve VIII hearing: whisper into each ear with the other occluded; any suspected loss needs formal audiologic testing to confirm it and tell conductive from sensorineural loss (Weber and Rinne can be tried at the bedside but are hard to do well outside specialized settings).
claims.quote: Hearing is first tested in each ear by whispering something while occluding the opposite ear. Any suspected loss should prompt formal audiologic testing to confirm findings and differentiate conductive hearing loss from sensorineural hearing loss. The Weber and Rinne tests may be done at the bedside to attempt to differentiate the two, but they are difficult to do effectively except in specialized settings.

claims.text: Nystagmus clues: nystagmus that changes direction is probably central (its absence does not exclude a central cause); peripheral nystagmus beats away from the dysfunctional side.
claims.quote: If nystagmus changes direction (eg, from 1 side to the other when, for example, the direction of gaze changes), it is probably central. However, absence of this finding does not exclude central causes. If nystagmus is peripheral, the eyes beat away from the dysfunctional side.

claims.text: Cranial nerves IX and X: the palate should rise symmetrically on "ah"; with one paretic side the uvula is pulled away from it; bilateral absent gag reflex is common in healthy people, especially older adults.
claims.quote: Whether the palate elevates symmetrically when the patient says "ah" is noted. If 1 side is paretic, the uvula is lifted away from the paretic side. A tongue blade can be used to touch 1 side of the posterior pharynx, then the other, and symmetry of the gag reflex is observed; bilateral absence of the gag reflex is common among healthy people, especially in older adults, and may not be significant.

claims.text: Isolated hoarseness: with normal gag and palatal elevation, look for a lesion (e.g. mediastinal lymphoma, aortic aneurysm) compressing the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
claims.quote: Once isolated hoarseness (with normal gag and palatal elevation) has been confirmed, the clinician should search for lesions (eg, mediastinal lymphoma, aortic aneurysm) compressing the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

claims.text: Cranial nerve XI: turning the head against resistance tests the sternocleidomastoid (felt opposite the side the head turns to); shrugging against resistance tests the upper trapezius.
claims.quote: For the sternocleidomastoid, the patient is asked to turn the head to 1 side and then maintain that position against resistance supplied by the examiner’s hand while the examiner palpates the active muscle (opposite the side to which the head is turned). For the upper trapezius, the patient is asked to elevate the shoulders against resistance supplied by the examiner.

claims.text: Cranial nerve XII: inspect the protruded tongue for atrophy, fasciculations and weakness; it deviates toward the side of the lesion.
claims.quote: The hypoglossal cranial nerve (XII) is evaluated by asking the patient to extend the tongue and inspecting it for atrophy, fasciculations, and weakness (deviation is toward the side of a lesion).
